title: The Power of the Humdrum: Why Your First Day of School Isn’t Going to Make or Break Your School Year ke-or-break-your-school-year/
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Recalling his own terror as a new Baltimore teacher who believed the first day set the tone for all 179 that follow, Stuart argues that first and last days matter far less than how teachers use the ordinary minutes in between. Quoting Practice Perfect on positive outliers who saw the power of the everyday, he says the humdrum minutes at the start, middle and end of lessons are 99 percent of the field where academic mastery is sown. He illustrates the point with a personal story about feeling hurried to buy a home, concluding that the real well-being of his family lives in today's ordinary moments rather than in one big outcome. The piece advises preparing for the first day but swatting away the anxious urge to treat it as decisive, and it ends with a brief nod to a classroom management course.
points: The belief that day one makes or breaks the year is challenged by the point that first and last days are special but not omnipotent.
Most of the opportunity for academic mastery lies in the routine minutes of every lesson, a view supported by Practice Perfect's study of outlier teachers.
The house-hunting anecdote shows the same hurry instinct at work in teaching: chasing the right moment distracts from the life being lived today.
Stuart's counsel is to prepare well for day one, then bring yourself back, day by day, to the power of the minutes available now.
quotes: Great teachers did more than obsess on the efficiency of their classroom — their questions were artful; their assignments, demanding — but there was a clear tendency among positive outliers to see the power of the humdrum, the everyday.

I don’t remember a thing about Dr. Wong’s presentation. This was no fault of his, of course; I was just too scared to listen, so full were my head and heart with the ringing truism that the first day of school sets the course for all the 179 or so that follow it.

Thirteen years later, I can tell you that while of course first days and last days are special, they’re not omnipotent — not even close. What’s far more critical is the way in which you’ll use all the minutes allotted to you this year.

What matters, in other words, is what we make of the “humdrum,” of the everyday, those little minutes at the start and end and middle of our lessons. Those are 99% of the field in which we’ll sow (or not) the seeds of academic mastery.
The power of living well and teaching well is only accessible now. The well-being of the Stuart family isn’t found in which home we live in — it’s found in today’s humdrum moments.
But when the little quibbling creature comes crawling on your shoulder, do swat it away with the truth that the power isn’t in the first day or the last — it’s in all the minutes in between.
